extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in graph theory, history of mathematics, and issues around computer-assisted proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards that appear in discussion of proofs of the four-color theorem, especially issues about what counts as a valid proof (graph-theoretic assumptions, case reductions, exhaustive computer checking, and community acceptance). Useful for evaluating or producing proofs or accounts of this theorem and related graph-coloring results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target statement: four-color theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that the chromatic number of every simple planar graph is at most four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restates Guthrie's original problem in graph terms: replace regions by vertices and adjacencies by edges; show every simple planar graph can be vertex-colored with ≤4 colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph domain requirements: simple and planar
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs that come from maps must be simple (no loops; at most one edge between two vertices) and planar (can be drawn with no crossing edges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the hypotheses under which the four-color statement is posed; proofs should explicitly use and preserve these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structural lemmas (existence of low-degree vertex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple planar graph contains at least one vertex with degree at most five (at most five neighbors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural fact enables inductive or reduction arguments (remove such a vertex to reduce to smaller graph). Proofs relying on induction typically start from this lemma and must justify it carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case reduction via vertex removal and recoloring (Kempe-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove a low-degree vertex, color the remainder (by induction), then extend the coloring to the removed vertex; if its neighbors use all four colors, use recoloring chains to free a color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kempe's method is an instructive template: prove base cases, remove a vertex of small degree, and when neighbor colors block an extension, perform controlled recolorings. Historical note: Kempe's recoloring argument had an overlooked special case that invalidated the proof, so modern implementations must check all subcases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive special-configuration checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that every simple planar graph contains one of a prescribed finite set of reducible configurations, and prove that any graph containing such a configuration is four-colorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appel and Haken reduced the problem to 1,936 special configurations; a valid proof must (for each listed configuration) demonstrate reducibility — i.e., that the existence of that configuration implies the graph can be colored with four colors. Because the number of cases can be enormous, this often requires systematic checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted exhaustive verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computers to carry out the large-scale, case-by-case checks required to verify that every possible configuration/case satisfies the needed property (e.g., reducibility or 4-colorability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appel and Haken's proof required over 1,000 hours of computer time. When proofs rely on extensive computation, authors should supply enough detail (algorithms, data, and results) to allow independent reruns or audits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-verifiability and transparency of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should ideally be "understandable and verifiable entirely by humans"; mathematicians historically resist ceding core logical reasoning to opaque computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While using computers for routine arithmetic was traditionally acceptable, proofs that depend on opaque computer logic face skepticism. To increase acceptance, authors should make the computational steps transparent, provide source code/data, explain the logical structure, and where possible separate human-checkable reasoning from routine computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and documentation for computational proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational components should be documented and reproducible so others can verify the computations underlying the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the heavy computer time used in some proofs, provide code, input data, and sufficient description so others can re-run the work; this mitigates concerns about errors in large automated case analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisations to other surfaces: Heawood bound
rubrics_metrics.description: For maps drawn on a surface of genus g (a doughnut with g holes), the maximum number of colors that may be needed is floor( (7 + sqrt(1 + 48g)) / 2 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending coloring problems to nonplanar surfaces, apply Heawood's theorem (with appropriate proof/completeness). Authors generalizing the planar case must state and use the correct genus-dependent bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-bound technique: complete subgraphs (K_n) give chromatic lower bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a graph contains a complete subgraph on n vertices (K_n), its chromatic number is at least n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of K_n minors/subgraphs as an immediate certificate that at least n colors are necessary. This is a standard tool to establish lower bounds on chromatic number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to conjectural criteria (Hadwiger's conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hadwiger's conjecture suggests a deeper criterion: if a graph has chromatic number n, it should contain a K_n minor; equivalently, absence of a K_n minor implies the graph is colorable with fewer than n colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While conjectural (open in general), Hadwiger's conjecture provides a conceptual standard and a target for generalizations of the four-color theorem; proofs/general results may be judged by how they relate to or progress toward such conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment moderation standards (site policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quanta Magazine moderates comments to facilitate an informed, substantive, civil conversation; abusive, profane, self-promotional, misleading, incoherent or off-topic comments will be rejected; moderators work during New York business hours and accept comments only in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit rubric governs acceptable reader comments on the article: keep remarks civil, substantive, on-topic, non-promotional, coherent, truthful, and in English; expect moderation during business hours.
